Indoor infrared cabins here start at $1,999, and most of them run on a standard 120V household outlet. That is the practical difference between an indoor infrared cabin and almost every other sauna we sell: no dedicated circuit, no concrete pad, no roof.

How this differs from the two collections either side of it

Our indoor saunas collection includes traditional rock-heater rooms, which run far hotter and do need a dedicated circuit. Our infrared saunas collection includes outdoor cabins, which need a level, load-rated foundation. This page is the overlap: infrared heat, installed inside, on the power you already have.

What to check before you buy

Infrared cabins run at 120 to 140°F, roughly forty degrees cooler than a traditional room, which is why sessions here run 30 to 45 minutes rather than 15. Canadian hemlock is the common wood at this price; cedar appears less often and costs more. Most units include chromotherapy lighting as a fitted feature rather than an upgrade.

Standard delivery is free to the lower 48 with no minimum and is curbside drop-off: the cabin arrives at the kerb and you move it inside. Inside delivery to any room is $600, and $1,800 covers inside delivery plus unboxing and full assembly. Most cabins here need assembling either way.

EMF is the specification worth reading closely, and manufacturers apply the tiers inconsistently and measure at different distances. See low EMF, ultra low EMF and near zero EMF, each of which states what its tier means in mG.
